stem: A 4-year-old boy has had a liver abscess and two lymph-node abscesses, each growing Staphylococcus aureus, and a lung lesion that grew Aspergillus. His mother's brother died of an infection in childhood. Flow cytometry with dihydrorhodamine shows no oxidation in his neutrophils, whereas his mother's neutrophils show two populations.
oneliner: 4M + staph liver and node abscesses + Aspergillus lung lesion + maternal uncle died young + no oxidation on dihydrorhodamine → which gene?
ask: Mutation of which gene is most likely responsible?

whyNot.A: ITGB2 (CD18) loss is leukocyte adhesion deficiency: **no pus**, high neutrophil counts; here abscesses form and the **burst is absent**
whyNot.B: LYST causes Chediak-Higashi: **giant granules, albinism**, neuropathy; the burst is normal
whyNot.C: MPO deficiency is **autosomal recessive** and mild, mostly Candida; it does not give **S aureus abscesses** or a **carrier mother with two populations**
whyNot.D: BTK is also X-linked but gives **agammaglobulinemia** with encapsulated bacteria, not **S aureus and Aspergillus abscesses**

answer: CYBB, encoding gp91phox of NADPH oxidase
why: **Absent oxidation** with **catalase-positive** organisms (S aureus, Aspergillus) is **chronic granulomatous disease**. The **X-linked** pattern (maternal uncle, carrier mother with two cell populations) points to **CYBB**, the gp91phox subunit. Roughly a third of cases are autosomal recessive (p47phox, from NCF1, is the commonest).

idea.rule: A boy with an affected maternal uncle has an X-linked recessive defect; know the X-linked immunodeficiencies.
also: BTK: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
CD40LG: hyper-IgM syndrome
WAS: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
IL2RG: X-linked SCID

note: Review: options made plain gene symbols (only the answer carried a protein label); MPO why-not no longer claims a normal oxidation test, since DHR can be abnormal in MPO deficiency.

stem: A 66-year-old man has multiple myeloma. Cytogenetics of his plasma cells show a translocation that places an oncogene next to the enhancer of the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene. The same chromosome is involved in translocations of Burkitt lymphoma and follicular lymphoma.
oneliner: 66M + multiple myeloma + oncogene moved beside Ig heavy-chain enhancer + same partner in Burkitt and follicular lymphoma → which chromosome?
ask: On which chromosome is the immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene found?

whyNot.A: The **MHC** (HLA) genes are here, not the heavy-chain locus
whyNot.B: Carries **MYC** (the Burkitt partner), not the heavy-chain locus
whyNot.C: Carries **cyclin D1** (CCND1), the mantle cell and myeloma partner

why: The **heavy-chain locus is on chromosome 14**, so t(8;14), t(14;18) and t(11;14) all put an oncogene (**MYC, BCL2, cyclin D1**) beside the strong heavy-chain enhancer. The light-chain loci are **kappa on 2** and **lambda on 22**.

idea.rule: Heavy chain 14, kappa 2, lambda 22: Ig translocations use chromosome 14 for heavy chain.
also: t(8;14): MYC in Burkitt lymphoma
t(14;18): BCL2 in follicular lymphoma
t(11;14): cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma
t(8;22) and t(2;8): MYC with lambda or kappa in Burkitt variants

stem: A 16-year-old girl develops nonpitting swelling of the lips and tongue with hoarseness a few hours after a tooth extraction. She has had attacks of crampy abdominal pain, with no hives or itching, and antihistamines have not helped before. Her mother has similar attacks. Her C4 level is low between attacks.
oneliner: 16F + nonpitting lip and tongue swelling after tooth extraction + abdominal pain attacks + no hives + mother similar + low C4 → which gene?
ask: A mutation in which gene most likely causes this condition?

whyNot.A: Encodes **alpha-1 antitrypsin**; deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease, not swelling attacks
whyNot.B: Encodes **pyrin**; familial Mediterranean fever gives **fever and serositis**, with no lip or airway swelling
whyNot.C: C1q deficiency causes **lupus-like disease** and pyogenic infections, not swelling attacks
whyNot.D: C4 deficiency gives **lupus-like disease**; her C4 is low only because uncontrolled C1 **consumes** it

why: **Nonpitting, non-itchy swelling** triggered by trauma, with **abdominal pain** and a dominant family history, is **hereditary angioedema**. Types I and II are **autosomal dominant** mutations of **SERPING1**, the gene for **C1 esterase inhibitor**. Without it, **bradykinin** rises and **C4 and C2** are consumed.

idea.rule: Hereditary angioedema = autosomal dominant SERPING1 (C1 inhibitor); excess bradykinin causes swelling.
also: ACE inhibitors can trigger bradykinin swelling in anyone
Treat acute attacks with C1 inhibitor, icatibant or ecallantide, not epinephrine or antihistamines
Danazol raises C1 inhibitor production
Low C4 is the screening test

note: Review: stem rewritten (10-word run matched IMMUNO-0081); patient changed to 16F to differ from f-hae-comp-1-im; options made plain gene symbols.

stem: A 3-year-old girl has fever and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. A node biopsy grows Mycobacterium avium and shows sheets of histiocytes full of acid-fast bacilli but no well-formed granulomas. Her immunoglobulins and T- and B-cell counts are normal.
oneliner: 3F + M. avium in nodes + histiocytes full of bacilli, poorly formed granulomas + normal immunoglobulins and lymphocyte counts → which defect?
ask: Which gene product is most likely defective?

whyNot.B: Gives **S aureus and Aspergillus abscesses** with granulomas; here the only organism is **M avium** with poor granulomas
whyNot.C: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives **pus-free bacterial infections**, not mycobacteria filling macrophages
whyNot.D: X-linked SCID has **low T cells** and fails to thrive; her **counts are normal**
whyNot.E: Causes **agammaglobulinemia** with infections by encapsulated bacteria; her **immunoglobulins are normal**

why: Intracellular mycobacteria are controlled by a loop in which macrophages release **IL-12**, T and NK cells respond with **IFN-gamma**, and IFN-gamma **activates macrophages**. A defect in the **IFN-gamma receptor** (or IL-12 receptor or STAT1) leaves macrophages unable to kill, causing **disseminated atypical mycobacterial or BCG infection** with **poor granulomas** and normal immunoglobulins and counts.

idea.rule: Disseminated atypical mycobacteria or BCG with normal immunoglobulins means a break in the IL-12/IFN-gamma loop.
also: IL-12 receptor beta-1 deficiency
STAT1 defects
IFN-gamma is the key cytokine activating macrophages for granulomas
Anti-TNF drugs also risk granuloma failure and TB reactivation

stem: In a rat skin wound model, the wound bed is hypoxic and quickly fills with many new capillaries that are leaky, with local edema. Treating the wounds with a neutralizing antibody against one growth factor markedly reduces new vessel sprouting and edema, while collagen deposition and epithelial coverage are unaffected.
oneliner: Experiment + hypoxic wound with many new leaky capillaries and edema + antibody against one factor abolishes vessels, not collagen or epithelium → which growth factor?

whyNot.A: Drives **fibroblast collagen synthesis** and scarring; collagen deposition was **unaffected**
whyNot.B: Recruits **fibroblasts and smooth muscle**; collagen would have fallen
whyNot.E: An **anti-inflammatory** cytokine; it does not drive vessel growth

why: **Hypoxia**, through **HIF-1**, raises **VEGF**, which drives **endothelial sprouting and proliferation** and also **raises vascular permeability**, giving leaky new vessels and edema. Blocking it stopped **only the vessels and edema**, while collagen (TGF-beta, PDGF) and epithelial cover (EGF) went on normally.

idea.rule: VEGF = new vessels and leakiness, switched on by hypoxia.
also: Bevacizumab and ranibizumab block VEGF in cancer and wet macular degeneration
Tumors use VEGF to build their blood supply
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is driven by VEGF
Preeclampsia: placental sFlt-1 traps VEGF, injuring endothelium

note: Review: moved from phys to gene (card names a molecule); chain folded into why.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease from diabetes is evaluated for a living transplant. Her healthy 38-year-old brother, born to the same two parents, offers to donate. The HLA genes sit close together on chromosome 6, so each child inherits one block (haplotype) from each parent with little crossing over.
oneliner: 41F + end-stage kidney disease + full brother offers a kidney + HLA inherited as one haplotype from each parent → chance he is HLA-identical?
ask: What is the probability that her brother is HLA-identical to her (shares both haplotypes)?

whyNot.A: Both children draw from the **same two parents**, so inheriting the same pair of haplotypes is possible
whyNot.C: This is the chance a full sibling shares **exactly one** haplotype, a half match
whyNot.D: This is the chance of sharing **at least one** haplotype (25% + 50%), not both
whyNot.E: Only a **parent** is guaranteed to share a haplotype, and that is one haplotype, not two

answer: 25% (1 in 4): siblings are HLA-identical 25%, haploidentical 50%, fully mismatched 25%
why: Each parent passes **one of two haplotypes**, so the brother matches her paternal haplotype with probability 1/2 and her maternal haplotype with probability 1/2. Both match with probability **1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4**. Sharing exactly one is **1/2** and sharing none is **1/4**.

idea.rule: HLA haplotypes are inherited en bloc and codominantly, one from each parent; full siblings are 25% identical, 50% haploidentical, 25% mismatched.
also: A parent and child always share exactly one haplotype (haploidentical)
Identical twins share both haplotypes (100%)
An HLA-identical sibling is the preferred related donor for bone marrow transplant
Unrelated donors are matched by typing, not by descent

stem: Naive CD4 T cells from a healthy volunteer are cultured with antigen, antigen-presenting cells and IL-12. The cells go on to secrete large amounts of interferon-γ.
oneliner: Naive CD4 T cells + IL-12 in culture → IFN-γ-secreting cells → which transcription factor?
ask: Which transcription factor most directly programs this T-helper lineage?

whyNot.B: Master regulator of **Th2** cells, driven by IL-4, not by IL-12
whyNot.C: The signal transducer downstream of the **IL-4 receptor**; IL-12 uses a different STAT
whyNot.D: Defines **Th17** cells, which need IL-6 and TGF-β rather than IL-12
whyNot.E: Defines **regulatory T cells**, which make no IFN-γ

answer: T-bet (TBX21), induced via IL-12 receptor signalling through STAT4
why: **IL-12** signals through **STAT4** to induce **T-bet**, the master regulator of the **Th1** program. Th1 cells make **interferon-γ**, which activates macrophages against intracellular microbes. T-bet also reinforces IFN-γ production in a positive loop.

idea.rule: Each T-helper subset has a driving cytokine, a STAT, and a master transcription factor.
also: IL-12 → STAT4 → T-bet → Th1 (IFN-γ)
IL-4 → STAT6 → GATA-3 → Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13)
IL-6 + TGF-β → STAT3 → RORγt → Th17 (IL-17)
TGF-β + IL-2 → STAT5 → FOXP3 → regulatory T cells
